t: What finance is: money, time and risk
s: F00 · Finance studies how people, businesses and governments raise, allocate and manage money over time, under uncertainty. Learn why a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, how to move an amount forward or back in time, how to put a number on an uncertain outcome, and where finance does its work.
x: Finance Time value of money Interest rate Compounding Future value Present value Discounting Discount rate Risk Expected value Risk aversion Risk premium Risk-free rate Personal finance Corporate finance Investment finance Public finance Investment decision Capital budgeting Financing decision Financial system Define finance and explain why time and risk sit at the centre of almost every financial decision. Calculate the future value of an amount today and the present value of an amount received later, over whole years. Calculate the expected value of a simple uncertain outcome and explain a risk premium as compensation for bearing risk. Distinguish personal, corporate, investment and public finance by who makes the decisions and what they decide. Describe the three financial decisions every firm makes and the role finance plays in an economy.

s: F00 · Accounting records what has happened, economics explains how people and whole economies behave, and finance decides what to do next with money. Learn what each field asks of the same decision, how finance turns accounting records into forecasts, and what people in each field do.
x: Accounting Economics Scarcity Microeconomics Macroeconomics Inflation Opportunity cost Financial statements Financial accounting Managerial accounting Cash flow Depreciation Accounting profit Operating cash flow Economic profit Controller Certified public accountant CFO Distinguish finance, accounting and economics by the question each asks, the period it looks at and what it produces. Distinguish financial accounting from managerial accounting by their users, rules and purpose. Distinguish microeconomics from macroeconomics and identify the economic conditions that matter to a financial decision. Explain how finance uses accounting data, and calculate accounting profit, operating cash flow and economic profit for a simple business. Apply all three perspectives to one business decision and describe typical careers in each field.

s: F00 · Almost every financial decision, from a household budget to a company’s biggest investment, rests on six principles: time value, risk and return, cash over profit, incremental cash flows, diversification and no arbitrage. Learn what each says, why it holds, and how to apply it to Ana’s first decisions about Lantern.
x: Incremental cash flow Sunk cost Sunk cost fallacy Diversification Unsystematic risk Systematic risk Law of one price Arbitrage State the six principles of financial decision-making and explain the reasoning behind each. Apply the time value of money and the trade-off between risk and return to compare choices. Distinguish cash flow from accounting profit and explain how a profitable business can run short of cash. Identify the incremental cash flows of a decision, including opportunity costs, and exclude sunk costs and unchanged costs. Explain how diversification reduces risk and why it cannot remove risk that affects the whole economy. Explain the law of one price and calculate the profit from a simple arbitrage.

s: F00 · Where a business’s money comes from (debt and equity), and whether it can pay its bills when they fall due. Learn the words professionals use for both, calculate working capital and the current ratio, and see why a business can be worth a lot and still run out of cash.
x: Capital Debt Equity Interest Principal Default Cost of capital Capital structure Leverage Debt-to-equity ratio Liquidity Solvency Emergency fund Current asset Current liability Working capital Current ratio Quick ratio Define capital and distinguish debt from equity by the claim each gives, the risk each carries and what each costs a business in principle. Explain why debt magnifies the returns to shareholders in both good years and bad. Distinguish the liquidity of an asset from the liquidity of a firm, and liquidity from solvency. Calculate working capital, the current ratio and the quick ratio, and interpret what they do and do not show. Assess the liquidity of a person or a small business, including Ana’s emergency fund.

s: F00 · Book value, market value, market capitalisation, enterprise value, EBITDA and the multiples built from them: the words analysts use to say what a company is worth. Learn to calculate each one for Harbourline Roasters, to say what it leaves out, and to see why every valuation rests on assumptions.
x: Valuation Book value of equity Market value Market capitalisation Market-to-book ratio Enterprise value Net debt EBIT D&A Amortisation EBITDA Valuation multiple EV/EBITDA Earnings per share P/E ratio Distinguish book value from market value, and explain why the two usually differ. Calculate market capitalisation and enterprise value, and explain why enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash. Calculate EBIT and EBITDA from an income statement, and explain what EBITDA leaves out. Calculate and interpret the EV/EBITDA and P/E multiples, matching each numerator with the right measure of earnings. Estimate a value range from peer multiples and explain how the result depends on the assumptions chosen.

s: F00 · Interest is what money earns over time; inflation is what time takes away. Learn simple and compound interest, why compounding frequency matters, how an APR differs from an effective annual rate, and how to turn a nominal return into a real one, so you can tell whether savings are really growing.
x: Simple interest Compound interest Compounding frequency Effective annual rate APR Annual percentage yield Inflation Price index Consumer Price Index Purchasing power Nominal return Real return Real interest rate Calculate simple and compound interest, and explain why compounding makes balances grow faster over time. Calculate future values with more than one compounding period a year, and convert a quoted annual rate into an effective annual rate. Distinguish an APR (a quoted annual rate) from an effective annual rate, and compare two rates quoted on different bases. Explain inflation and purchasing power, and calculate an inflation rate from a price index. Calculate a real return exactly and by approximation, and recognise when the approximation fails.

s: F00 · Financial markets move savings to the people and firms who can put them to work, set prices for risk and time, and let investors sell when they need cash. Learn the main ways to sort them: direct or through an intermediary, new issues or resale, short or long term, what is traded, and where.
x: Financial market Financial assets Security Issuer Price discovery Direct finance Indirect finance Financial intermediary Interest-rate spread Primary market Initial public offering Secondary market Money market Capital market Equity market Bond market Bond Foreign-exchange market Commodity market Derivatives market Hedging Exchange Over-the-counter market Explain the four jobs financial markets do: channelling savings to investment, discovering prices, providing liquidity and sharing risk. Distinguish direct finance from indirect finance, and calculate an intermediary’s interest-rate spread. Classify a transaction as primary or secondary, and an instrument as belonging to the money market or the capital market. Describe what is traded in equity, bond, foreign-exchange, commodity and derivatives markets, and convert an amount between currencies. Compare exchanges with over-the-counter markets.

s: F00 · Banks, investment banks, pension funds, insurers, mutual funds, hedge funds, brokers and dealers each do a different job in moving money and risk, and central banks and regulators set the rules they work under. Learn who does what, how each is paid, and what the protections such as deposit insurance do and do not cover.
x: Commercial bank Bank run Investment bank Underwriting Underwriting spread Net proceeds Lock-up Institutional investors Pension fund Mutual fund Exchange-traded fund Net asset value Hedge fund Short selling Broker Dealer Market maker Bid Ask Bid-ask spread Federal Reserve SEC FDIC Ownership category Identify households, firms and governments as savers and borrowers, and describe the job of each kind of financial institution. Distinguish commercial banks from investment banks, and brokers from dealers and market makers. Compare pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds and hedge funds by whose money they manage and how investors get it back. Calculate a bid-ask spread, the net proceeds of a share offering and a fund’s net asset value per share. Describe what the Federal Reserve, the SEC, FINRA, the CFTC and the FDIC do, and calculate how much of a deposit FDIC insurance covers.

s: F00 · When the people who run a business are not the people who own it or lend to it, their interests can pull apart. Learn why that happens, what it costs, and the tools (boards, incentive pay, loan covenants, disclosure) used to keep managers working for the people whose money they use.
x: Separation of ownership and control Principal (agency) Agent Agency problem Agency costs Risk shifting Covenants Board of directors Incentive pay Stock options Shareholder view Stakeholder view Explain the separation of ownership and control and the principal-agent relationship it creates. Identify the main conflicts between shareholders and managers and between shareholders and lenders. Calculate how a manager’s ownership stake changes who bears the cost of a perk, and how risk-shifting moves value from lenders to shareholders. Describe what a board of directors does and evaluate incentive pay, including its side effects. Compare the shareholder and stakeholder views of what a company is for. Apply loan covenants and governance tools to Lantern Coffee as it takes on outside investors and debt.

t: What accounting is and why businesses need it
s: F01 · Accounting turns what happens to a business into information that owners, lenders, investors and governments can act on. Learn who relies on that information, the four statements it produces, who writes the rules, and the concepts that make the numbers worth trusting.
x: Accounting Financial accounting Managerial accounting Tax accounting GAAP IFRS FASB IASB SEC Conceptual framework Relevance Materiality Faithful representation Economic entity assumption Going concern assumption Monetary unit assumption Time period assumption Historical cost principle Full disclosure principle Financial statements Audit Explain accounting as an information system that identifies, records and communicates the economic events of a business. Identify the main users of accounting information and the decisions each one makes with it. Distinguish financial, managerial and tax accounting by their users, rules and purpose. Describe the question each of the four financial statements answers. Explain who sets accounting standards in the United States and internationally, and what the conceptual framework is for. Apply the qualitative characteristics, the four basic assumptions and the basic principles to everyday reporting decisions.

s: F01 · An account is where a business keeps every increase and decrease in one item. Learn the five kinds of account, how accounts are grouped as current or noncurrent and as permanent or temporary, and how a chart of accounts organises them.
x: Account Asset Liability Equity Revenue Expense Current asset Noncurrent asset Current liability Noncurrent liability Operating cycle Contra account Chart of accounts Permanent account Temporary account Common stock Explain what an account is and why a business keeps a separate account for each item it tracks. Classify accounts as assets, liabilities, equity, revenue or expenses, using the definitions in the FASB and IASB conceptual frameworks. Classify assets and liabilities as current or noncurrent, and accounts as permanent or temporary. Explain how a contra account works, using accumulated depreciation as the example. Read and extend a chart of accounts, recognising the US and IFRS or UK names for the same items. Justify the classification of borderline items such as prepaid insurance, unearned revenue and the current portion of a loan.

s: F01 · Every business’s resources come from creditors or owners, so assets always equal liabilities plus equity. Learn to trace any transaction through that equation and to see how revenue, expenses and dividends change what the owners own.
x: Accounting equation Net assets Dual aspect Unearned revenue Contributed capital Retained earnings Dividends Net income Expanded accounting equation Executory contract State the accounting equation and explain why it must balance after every transaction. Analyse a business transaction into its effects on assets, liabilities and equity. Use the expanded accounting equation to show how revenue, expenses and dividends change equity. Distinguish contributed capital from retained earnings. Calculate a missing element of the equation, including net income, from beginning and ending balances.

s: F01 · Debit means the left side of an account and credit means the right, nothing more. Work out from the accounting equation which side increases each kind of account, read normal balances, and calculate the balance of any T-account.
x: Debit Credit T-account Normal balance Double-entry bookkeeping Account balance Explain what debit and credit mean in bookkeeping, and why neither means good or bad. Explain, from the accounting equation, why each kind of account increases on the side it does. State the normal balance of assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses, dividends and contra-asset accounts. Calculate the balance of a T-account, and find a missing figure from the other three. Interpret a bank statement’s debits and credits from the bank’s point of view.

s: F01 · Every entry starts with a document and ends with a balanced record. Decide whether an event belongs in the books, analyse it in five steps, and write it in general journal form, including entries with more than two lines.
x: Source document Journal General journal Journal entry Compound entry Journalising Transaction analysis Identify the source document behind a transaction, and decide whether an event should be recorded at all. Analyse a transaction in five steps, from naming the accounts to checking that debits equal credits. Record simple and compound entries in general journal format, with dates, indented credits and explanations. Journalise Lantern Coffee’s March transactions. Diagnose common journalising errors, including the ones a balanced entry can hide.

s: F01 · The journal tells the story in date order; the general ledger sorts the same amounts by account so that every balance can be read. Learn to post each journal line, cross-reference the two records so any amount can be traced, keep running balances, and check customer and supplier detail against its control account.
x: General ledger Posting Posting reference Balance-column account Subsidiary ledger Control account Explain why a business keeps both a journal and a general ledger, and what each is for. Post journal entries to ledger accounts, writing posting references in both the journal and the ledger. Calculate an account’s balance in T-account form and in balance-column (running-balance) form. Reconcile a subsidiary ledger of customers or suppliers with its control account. Trace an amount between the ledger and the journal, and locate common posting errors. Distinguish what accounting software does automatically from the judgements it leaves to people.

s: F01 · List every ledger balance in a debit or a credit column and the two totals should agree. Learn to prepare a trial balance, to use the gap between the totals to track down mistakes, and to recognise the errors that a trial balance in perfect balance can still hide.
x: Trial balance Unadjusted trial balance Transposition error Slide error Compensating error Error of omission Error of commission Error of principle Error of original entry Reversal of entries Prepare a trial balance from ledger balances, listing accounts in chart order with each balance in its debit or credit column. Explain why the two columns must agree, and what a balancing trial balance does and does not prove. Identify errors a trial balance cannot detect: omissions, wrong accounts, reversals, compensating errors, and entries recorded twice or at the same wrong amount on both sides. Locate an error from the difference between the column totals, using the halving test and the test for divisibility by 9. Distinguish the unadjusted, adjusted and post-closing trial balances, and explain why none of them is a financial statement.

s: F01 · Profit and cash run on different clocks. Learn when revenue and expenses belong to a period under the accrual basis, how that differs from the cash basis, and how deferrals and accruals set up the month-end adjustments.
x: Cash basis Accrual basis Revenue recognition principle Expense recognition principle Performance obligation Deferral Accrual Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis and calculate profit under each for the same period. Apply the revenue recognition principle, including the five-step model of ASC 606 and IFRS 15, to decide when revenue is earned. Apply the expense recognition principle and explain what “matching” does and does not justify. Classify a gap between cash and recognition as a deferral or an accrual of revenue or expense. Reconcile cash-basis profit to accrual-basis net income item by item. Explain why US GAAP and IFRS financial statements use the accrual basis and where the cash basis is still used.

s: F01 · Some changes arrive without a transaction: insurance expires, wages build up, equipment wears. Learn to find, calculate and record the five kinds of month-end adjustment, and to prepare the adjusted trial balance that the financial statements are built from.
x: Adjusting entry Prepaid expense Accrued revenue Accrued expense Depreciation Accumulated depreciation Book value Straight-line method Residual value Useful life Adjusted trial balance Explain why adjusting entries are needed at the end of each period and why they never involve Cash. Record adjusting entries for prepaid expenses, unearned revenue, accrued revenue, accrued expenses and depreciation. Calculate straight-line depreciation, accumulated depreciation and book value, including for part of a year. Calculate accrued interest with I = P × r × t. Prepare an adjusted trial balance from an unadjusted trial balance and the adjusting entries. Analyse the effect of omitting an adjustment on net income, assets, liabilities and equity.

t: Financial statements from the adjusted trial balance
s: F01 · Turn Lantern’s adjusted trial balance into an income statement, a statement of changes in equity, a classified balance sheet and a statement of cash flows, see how the four fit together, and read what they say about Lantern’s first month.
x: Income statement Statement of changes in equity Statement of retained earnings Balance sheet Classified balance sheet Statement of cash flows Operating activities Investing activities Financing activities Articulation Prepare a single-step income statement from an adjusted trial balance. Prepare a statement of changes in equity and a statement of retained earnings. Prepare a classified balance sheet, presenting a contra-asset correctly. Prepare a statement of cash flows by the direct method, classifying each cash flow as operating, investing or financing. Explain how the four statements articulate and check that they do. Interpret a small business’s statements: its profit, where its cash came from and how it is financed.

s: F01 · At the end of a period, the revenue, expense and dividend accounts are emptied into Retained Earnings so that the next period starts from zero. Learn the four closing entries, record Lantern’s for March, and prove the result with a post-closing trial balance.
x: Closing entries Income Summary Post-closing trial balance Distinguish temporary accounts, which are closed at the end of each period, from permanent accounts, which carry their balances forward. Explain the two jobs closing entries do: resetting the temporary accounts and bringing Retained Earnings up to date. Record the four closing entries through Income Summary, for a net income and for a net loss. Prepare a post-closing trial balance and use it to confirm that only permanent accounts remain open. Calculate retained earnings after closing and reconcile it with the statement of changes in equity and the balance sheet. Identify common closing errors and correct them.

s: F01 · Every period, every business runs the same nine steps, from analysing a transaction to proving that the ledger is ready for the next period. See the whole cycle at once, use the optional worksheet and reversing entries, correct errors after posting, and protect the records with internal control.
x: Accounting cycle Worksheet Reversing entry Correcting entry Internal control Segregation of duties List the nine steps of the accounting cycle in order, and say which happen during the period and which at its end. Record reversing entries for accruals and show that they lead to the same balances as recording without them. Record correcting entries for errors found after posting: a wrong account, a wrong amount and an omitted entry. Explain what internal control is, and apply segregation of duties, authorisation, documentation, physical safeguards and reconciliations to a small business. Apply the whole cycle to a small business, from its first transaction to its post-closing trial balance. Distinguish the steps that accounting software automates from the judgements it cannot make.

s: F02 · Decide when revenue is earned and how much to record by working through the five steps of ASC 606 and IFRS 15: deposits and prepaid subscriptions, bundles, refunds, discounts and the question of gross or net. Then reconcile Lantern’s online-shop order values with the revenue in its books.
x: Contract liability Contract asset Transaction price Variable consideration Stand-alone selling price Control Contra-revenue account Sales Returns and Allowances Sales discount Refund liability Principal (in a sale) Agent (in a sale) Net revenue Apply the five steps of ASC 606 and IFRS 15 to a contract, using the control criteria to decide whether revenue is recognised over time or at a point in time. Calculate the share of a transaction price allocated to each performance obligation, in proportion to stand-alone selling prices. Record contract liabilities (unearned revenue), receivables, refunds and sales discounts, and present contra-revenue accounts correctly. Distinguish a principal from an agent and explain how the answer changes reported revenue. Reconcile Lantern’s online-shop order values with the revenue, unearned revenue and cash in its books.

t: Inventory and cost of goods sold
s: F02 · Follow the cost of the bags Lantern sells from the roaster’s invoice to the income statement: what goes into inventory, perpetual and periodic records, the FIFO, LIFO and weighted average formulas, the lower of cost and net realisable value, and what each choice does to gross profit, tax and the balance sheet.
x: Merchandising business Inventory Cost of goods sold Goods available for sale Perpetual inventory system Periodic inventory system Shrinkage Freight-in FIFO LIFO Weighted average cost LIFO conformity rule Net realisable value Lower of cost and net realisable value Inventory write-down Gross profit Gross margin Explain how the cost of goods moves from inventory, an asset, to cost of goods sold, an expense, under perpetual and periodic systems. Calculate cost of goods sold and ending inventory by FIFO, LIFO and weighted average, and with beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory. Compare the effects of the cost formulas on gross profit, income tax and the balance sheet when purchase costs rise, including the LIFO conformity rule and IFRS’s prohibition of LIFO. Apply the lower of cost and net realisable value under US GAAP and IFRS, including whether a write-down may be reversed. Analyse the effect of an error in ending inventory on two years’ income statements and balance sheets.

s: F02 · Rebuild Lantern’s first-year income statement in stages: net revenue, cost of sales and gross profit, operating expenses and operating income, interest, income tax and net income. Then calculate EBIT and EBITDA, see the rules for presenting non-GAAP measures, and meet earnings per share.
x: Single-step income statement Multi-step income statement Cost of sales Cost of services Operating expenses Operating income Other income and expenses Income tax expense Statutory tax rate Effective tax rate Function of expense method Nature of expense method Non-GAAP financial measure Adjusted EBITDA Basic earnings per share Diluted earnings per share Prepare a multi-step income statement from an adjusted trial balance, and explain how it differs from a single-step statement. Calculate gross profit, gross margin, operating income, income before income tax, income tax expense and net income. Classify expenses by function and by nature, and place each account in the right section of a multi-step statement. Calculate EBIT and EBITDA from an income statement, and explain the SEC rules for presenting EBITDA as a non-GAAP measure. Calculate basic earnings per share and state which companies must report it.

s: F02 · Selling on credit creates receivables, and some of them will never be paid. Learn the allowance method that US GAAP and IFRS require, estimate bad debts by aging and by a percentage of sales, account for notes receivable, and build up a business’s current liabilities, using Lantern’s first year-end.
x: Accounts receivable Credit terms Bad debt expense Allowance for doubtful accounts Allowance method Direct write-off method Write-off Aging of receivables Expected credit losses Net receivables Note receivable Accounts payable Accrued liability Income taxes payable Explain why US GAAP and IFRS require the allowance method for receivables, what the CECL model (ASC 326) asks for, and why the direct write-off method is acceptable only for immaterial amounts. Calculate the allowance for doubtful accounts by aging receivables and by a percentage of credit sales, and the bad debt expense when the allowance has a credit or a debit balance before adjustment. Record credit sales, collections, write-offs, recoveries and the year-end bad debt adjustment, and report receivables net of the allowance. Calculate the interest on a note receivable and record its accrual and collection. Identify and measure a business’s current liabilities (accounts payable, accrued liabilities, unearned revenue and income taxes payable) and assemble them for the balance sheet.

s: F02 · Equipment, vehicles, buildings and patents help a business earn revenue for years, so their cost is spread over those years. Learn what goes into an asset’s cost, how to depreciate it by three methods, what to do when estimates change or the asset is sold, how intangible assets and goodwill are treated, and where US GAAP and IFRS part company.
x: Property, plant and equipment Intangible asset Capitalise Depreciable amount Double-declining-balance method Units-of-production method Change in accounting estimate Gain on disposal Patent Goodwill Impairment Revaluation model Component depreciation Determine the cost of a long-lived asset by deciding which expenditures to capitalise and which to expense. Calculate depreciation by the straight-line, double-declining-balance and units-of-production methods, including part years under a stated convention. Record depreciation, a change in an accounting estimate and the disposal of an asset with a gain or loss. Calculate the amortisation of a patent, and explain how goodwill is treated by public and private companies under US GAAP and under IFRS. Compare US GAAP and IFRS on revaluation, component depreciation and impairment.

s: F02 · Put Lantern’s year-end balances into a classified balance sheet: decide what is current, split a loan into its current and noncurrent parts, and calculate working capital and the current ratio. Then look inside equity, at par value, additional paid-in capital, dividends and the statement of changes in equity.
x: Order of liquidity Current portion of long-term debt Report form Account form Authorised shares Outstanding shares Treasury stock Par value No-par stock Additional paid-in capital Declaration date Date of record Payment date Dividends payable Classify assets and liabilities as current or noncurrent under US GAAP and IFRS, including the current portion of long-term debt. Prepare a classified balance sheet in report form, with contra accounts shown on its face. Calculate working capital and the current ratio, and the effect on them of debt classification and of when a dividend is paid. Record the issue of par-value and no-par stock and the declaration and payment of a cash dividend. Prepare a statement of changes in equity and reconcile it with the balance sheet.

s: F02 · Prepare a full year’s statement of cash flows: decide what counts as cash, classify every receipt and payment under US GAAP and IFRS, work out the direct-method lines from the accrual records, and disclose what changed without any cash moving.
x: Cash equivalents Direct method Indirect method Noncash investing and financing activities Explain what the statement of cash flows reports, and decide which items are cash and cash equivalents. Classify receipts and payments as operating, investing or financing under US GAAP (ASC 230), and state how IAS 7 differs before and after the IFRS 18 amendments. Calculate direct-method operating cash flows from income statement figures and the changes in the related balance sheet accounts. Prepare a statement of cash flows by the direct method, with a disclosure of noncash investing and financing activities. Explain why ASC 230 encourages the direct method although most companies use the indirect method.

s: F02 · Start from net income and reach cash from operating activities: add back noncash expenses, take out gains and losses, adjust for every change in operating working capital, then prepare a full statement from two balance sheets and reconcile it with the direct method.
x: Noncash expense Add-back Operating working capital Explain why each adjustment in the indirect method is added or subtracted, using the accounting equation. Calculate net cash from operating activities by the indirect method, including noncash expenses, gains and losses, and changes in operating current assets and liabilities. Prepare a complete statement of cash flows from comparative balance sheets, an income statement and notes, including a disposal at a gain and a current portion of long-term debt. Reconcile the indirect method with the direct method, line by line. Identify and correct common errors, such as treating depreciation as a source of cash or reversing the sign of a working-capital change.

s: F02 · Put Lantern’s whole annual report together, check that its four statements articulate and find the error when they don’t, follow single transactions through all of them, see where the gap between profit and cash sits, and push one change through the three main statements the way analysts test a model.
x: Annual report Roll-forward Tie-out Three-statement model Trace a transaction through the income statement, the statement of changes in equity, the balance sheet and the statement of cash flows. Use a preparer’s checklist of links to test whether a set of statements articulates, and locate the error when a link fails. Locate each part of the gap between Lantern’s net income and its operating cash flow on the balance sheet, and judge which parts will reverse. Calculate the effect of one change, such as $1,000 more depreciation with tax at 25%, on all three main statements, with the tax paid or still owed. Interpret the linked statements to judge how much cash a business can afford to distribute.

s: F02 · Compare the two frameworks where they differ for the statements in this course (inventory, property, development costs, leases, cash-flow classification and, from 2027, the structure of the income statement), measure what each difference does to the figures, and see why Lantern reports under US GAAP.
x: Convergence Foreign private issuer Other comprehensive income Management-defined performance measure Public business entity Private Company Council Describe who sets US GAAP and IFRS, the SEC’s role, and how far the two frameworks converged. Classify each difference between the frameworks by what it changes: profit, assets and equity only, or presentation only. Calculate how a difference between the frameworks changes a company’s profit, assets or operating cash flow, and restate a profit figure from one framework to the other. Explain what IFRS 18 changes in the income statement and what ASU 2024-03 requires of US public business entities, with their effective dates. Identify the frameworks a US private company may use, and explain why Lantern uses US GAAP.

s: F04 · Interest is charged in one of two ways: on the principal only, or on the principal and the interest already earned. Learn to calculate both for any length of time, to count days the way loan contracts do, and to work backwards from two amounts to the rate or the time that links them.
x: Accrued interest Day-count convention Growth factor Compound annual growth rate Logarithm Doubling time Rule of 72 Calculate simple interest, and the interest accrued for part of a year under the actual/365, actual/360 and 30/360 day-count conventions. Calculate the future value of an amount under compound interest, including over a fractional number of periods. Find the compound rate that links two amounts over a given time, using an nth root. Calculate the time needed to reach a target using logarithms, and compare the exact doubling time with the rule of 72. Choose between simple and compound interest for a real arrangement, and explain why the choice changes the answer.

s: F04 · A rate of 7.2% a year can cost 7.2%, 7.40% or 7.47% a year depending on how often interest is compounded. Learn to tell nominal, periodic and effective rates apart, to convert any rate to any compounding frequency (continuous compounding included), to read a US annual percentage yield, and to compare offers quoted in different ways.
x: Nominal annual rate Periodic rate Equivalent rates Continuous compounding Early-payment discount Distinguish a nominal annual rate (APR), a periodic rate and an effective annual rate (EAR), and convert each into the others. Calculate the effective annual rate for any compounding frequency, including continuous compounding. Convert a rate quoted with one compounding frequency into the equivalent rate with another. Calculate an annual percentage yield (APY) as US banks disclose it under the Truth in Savings rules, and explain what it includes. Compare loan, deposit and trade-credit offers quoted on different bases, and choose the best one.

s: F04 · An amount of money has a different value at every date. Learn to draw a timeline, discount single amounts with discount factors, move any amount to any date, cope with rates that change, and solve for the missing amount, rate or time, so that amounts at different dates can be compared fairly.
x: Cash-flow timeline Discount factor Comparison date Equation of value Construct a cash-flow timeline for a single-amount problem and match the rate per period to the spacing of the periods. Calculate the present value of a future amount with a discount factor, for any compounding frequency and for amounts due between compounding dates. Compare and combine amounts due at different dates by moving them to a common comparison date, including when the rate changes from period to period. Find the unknown amount, rate or time in a single-amount problem with a formula, a financial calculator or a spreadsheet, and check the answer. Explain why present value falls as the rate or the time rises, and why distant amounts are far more sensitive to the rate than near ones.

s: F04 · Most real streams of money are uneven: a loan pays interest and then its principal, a project costs money now and returns different amounts later. Learn to value any stream by discounting each cash flow, to judge a decision by its net present value, and to find the rate of return that makes that value zero.
x: Cash-flow stream Net present value Internal rate of return NPV profile Face value Construct a timeline for an uneven stream of cash flows and calculate its present value, or its value at any other date, by discounting each flow. Calculate the net present value of a decision and use it to accept or reject the decision, explaining what a positive NPV means. Price a fixed-rate note at the current market rate and explain why its value moves in the opposite direction to interest rates. Estimate an internal rate of return by trial and interpolation, and explain how it relates to NPV and where it can mislead. Use spreadsheet NPV and IRR functions correctly, including the timing of the first cash flow.

s: F04 · Loan instalments, rent, leases, pensions and savings plans are all streams of equal payments. Learn to value such a stream in one step, whether the payments come at the end or the start of each period, start now or later, stay level or grow, and to solve for the payment, the number of payments or the rate.
x: Annuity Ordinary annuity Annuity due Annuity factor Deferred annuity Growing annuity Implied interest rate Calculate the present and future value of an ordinary annuity and of an annuity due, and explain why they differ by a factor of (1 + r). Calculate the value of a deferred annuity and of a growing annuity by moving the stream to a common date. Calculate the payment or the number of payments of an annuity, using logarithms for the number of payments. Find the interest rate of an annuity by trial and error or with a spreadsheet’s RATE function. Evaluate an instalment plan sold as “0% interest” by finding its present value and its implied interest rate.

s: F04 · A payment that never stops still has a finite value today. Learn to value level and growing perpetuities, including ones that start now or later, price a preferred share, size an endowment, and see why anything valued as growing forever depends so heavily on the gap between the discount rate and the growth rate.
x: Perpetuity Growing perpetuity Perpetuity due Endowment Preferred stock Gordon growth model Terminal value Calculate the present value of a level perpetuity, a perpetuity due and a deferred perpetuity. Calculate the present value of a growing perpetuity, and explain why it needs r > g and next period’s payment. Calculate the value of a preferred share and the gift needed to endow a payment forever, with or without growth. Analyse how the value of a growing perpetuity responds to small changes in the discount rate and the growth rate. Explain what a terminal value is, and estimate one for a simple forecast.

s: F04 · An instalment loan is an annuity seen from the borrower’s side. Learn to calculate the payment, build a schedule that splits each payment into interest and principal, find the balance owed at any date, and use those tools to compare loans and instalment plans, to judge prepaying or refinancing, and to see what fees do to the APR.
x: Interest-only loan Balloon payment Amortising loan Amortisation schedule Outstanding balance Prepayment Prepayment penalty Refinancing Finance charge Calculate the level payment on an amortising loan and the total interest it costs. Construct an amortisation schedule showing the interest, principal and balance for each payment. Calculate the balance outstanding after any payment by the prospective and the retrospective methods, and the interest paid between two dates. Compare an interest-only loan with an amortising loan, and a bank loan with an instalment plan, without being misled by total interest. Evaluate prepayment and refinancing, and calculate the APR of a loan with an up-front fee.

s: F04 · A dollar next year is not the same unit as a dollar today. Measure inflation over several years, convert amounts into today’s dollars, use the exact Fisher relation, and discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates, so that every comparison across time is made in one kind of dollar.
x: Nominal amount Real amount Base period Cumulative inflation Average annual inflation rate Fisher relation Escalation clause Deflation Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities Break-even inflation rate Calculate yearly, cumulative and average annual inflation from a price index over several years. Convert a nominal amount at any date into real dollars of a chosen base date, and back again. Apply the exact Fisher relation to find a real rate, a nominal rate or an inflation rate, using effective rates for the same period. Calculate the present value of a cash-flow stream both in nominal terms and in real terms, and explain why consistent discounting gives the same answer. Calculate the real growth of a salary or a price, and explain how Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) keep their purchasing power.

s: F04 · A home loan is an annuity with a house attached. Calculate a fixed-rate mortgage payment, compare 30- and 15-year terms, find the balance after any number of years, decide whether discount points and extra payments pay off, see what inflation does to a fixed payment, and read how an adjustable-rate mortgage resets.
x: Mortgage Fixed-rate mortgage Down payment Discount points Lender credit Escrow account Adjustable-rate mortgage Fully indexed rate Rate cap Calculate the monthly principal-and-interest payment, the total interest and the balance after k years on a fixed-rate mortgage. Compare a 30-year and a 15-year mortgage on payment, total interest and how fast the balance falls. Evaluate discount points by their simple break-even time and by the present value of the savings over the time the loan is kept. Calculate how much time and interest regular extra payments save, using logarithms to find the new term. Calculate the real value of a fixed mortgage payment under inflation, and the new payment when an adjustable-rate mortgage resets within its caps.

s: B01 · Analytics turns data into better decisions. Learn the four questions it answers (what happened, why, what will happen and what should we do), what each needs and produces, where machine learning fits, and the five-step process that runs from a business question to a measured result.
x: Analytics Business analytics Descriptive analytics Diagnostic analytics Predictive analytics Prescriptive analytics Forecast Forecast error Scenario Optimisation Machine learning Analytics process Define business analytics and explain how data, people and decisions work together in it. Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics by the question each answers, the methods it uses and what it produces. Classify a business question by the kind of analytics it needs, and explain why one decision usually draws on several kinds. Explain the trade-off between the value and the difficulty of the four kinds, and where that picture misleads. Calculate the expected value of a decision option and the error of a forecast, as simple instances of prescriptive and predictive work. Describe where machine learning fits and the five steps of the analytics process: question, data, analysis, decision and measure.

s: B01 · Most analyses that fail, fail at the first step: the question. Learn to turn a vague worry into a decision-focused question, a SMART objective and testable hypotheses, and to pin down exactly what counts, for whom, over what period and compared with what, before you open any data.
x: Decision-focused question SMART objective Hypothesis Operational definition Unit of analysis Baseline Time frame Stakeholder Distinguish a vague question from a decision-focused business question, and rewrite one as the other. Write a SMART objective, and test an objective against the five criteria. Write testable hypotheses and state the evidence that would support or contradict each. Write an operational definition for a business term such as an order, a customer or a visit, and calculate how the choice of definition changes a result. Identify the unit of analysis, time frame, comparison and threshold a question needs, and the stakeholders who should agree them.

s: B01 · Structure turns a big, messy problem into small questions that data can answer. Learn issue trees and the MECE test, driver trees that break revenue into visits, conversion and order value, root-cause tools such as the five whys and their limits, the CRISP-DM process, and how to tell when you have enough evidence to stop.
x: Issue tree MECE Hypothesis-driven analysis Exploratory data analysis Driver tree Root-cause analysis Root cause Five whys CRISP-DM Construct an issue tree for a business problem and test whether each level is mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE). Build a driver tree for revenue (visits × conversion rate × average order value) and calculate how much of a change each driver accounts for. Distinguish hypothesis-driven from exploratory analysis and choose between them for a given problem. Apply the five whys and a driver tree to look for a root cause, and explain the limits of each. Describe the six phases of CRISP-DM and relate them to the analytics process. Decide when to stop analysing, by weighing what more evidence could change against what it costs.

s: B01 · Before you can analyse data you have to say what kind it is: a table or free text, what one row describes, which columns are categories and which are amounts, how the data runs through time and who collected it. Each answer limits what you can sensibly calculate.
x: Structured data Semi-structured data Unstructured data Dataset Observation Variable Unit of observation Categorical variable Numerical variable Nominal variable Ordinal variable Interval variable Ratio variable Discrete variable Continuous variable Level of measurement Identifier Cross-sectional data Time-series data Panel data Primary data Secondary data Distinguish structured, semi-structured and unstructured data, and explain what has to happen before unstructured data can be counted. Identify the observations, variables and unit of observation of a dataset. Classify a variable as categorical (nominal or ordinal) or numerical (discrete or continuous), and by level of measurement, and state which summaries each level allows. Recognise identifiers and codes that are written with digits but are not amounts. Distinguish cross-sectional, time-series and panel data, and primary from secondary data, and choose the kind a question needs.

t: Collecting data: sources, samples and bias
s: B01 · How data was collected decides what it can show. Learn the main sources of business data, how a sample stands in for a population, the four biases that most often mislead (sampling, non-response, survivorship and measurement), how to word a survey question, and the basics of consent and privacy.
x: Transactional data Population Sample Census Sampling frame Simple random sample Convenience sample Self-selected sample Sampling error Sampling bias Non-response bias Survivorship bias Measurement bias Response rate A/B test Control group Personal data Consent Distinguish the main sources of business data (transactional and web data, surveys, experiments, observation, third-party and public data) and choose one that fits a question. Identify the population, sampling frame and sample of a study, and distinguish random from convenience sampling. Identify sampling, non-response, survivorship and measurement bias in a study, and explain which way each pushes a result. Calculate a response rate and the range within which non-response could place a survey result. Evaluate survey questions for leading, double-barrelled and unanswerable wording, and rewrite them. Describe in outline the consent and privacy rules that apply when a business collects personal data.

t: Data quality: is the data fit for the question?
s: B01 · Data can be wrong in different ways, and each way distorts a different number. Learn the six dimensions of data quality, how duplicates, gaps, invalid values, inconsistent codes and time zones move a metric, how to judge whether data is good enough for a purpose, and who is responsible for its quality. B02 then teaches the repairs.
x: Fitness for purpose Data quality dimension Accuracy Completeness Consistency Validity Timeliness Uniqueness Duplicate record Missing value UTC Data lifecycle Data owner Define the six dimensions of data quality (accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, timeliness and uniqueness) and give a business consequence of a failure in each. Explain how duplicates, missing values, invalid values, inconsistent codes and time zones distort a metric, and calculate the size of the distortion in simple cases. Assess whether a dataset is fit for a stated purpose, and say what would make it fit. Identify who produces, owns and uses data in a business, and where in the data lifecycle quality problems enter. Identify the quality problems in a raw export by dimension, without changing it.

s: B01 · A key performance indicator is a metric with a job: an exact formula, a target, a direction and an owner. Learn to define an online shop’s KPIs precisely, to tell counts from rates and leading from lagging indicators, and to build a balanced set of measures that is hard to game.
x: Metric Key performance indicator Conversion rate Average order value Lagging indicator Leading indicator Goodhart’s law Guardrail metric Balanced scorecard Dashboard Distinguish a metric from a key performance indicator (KPI), and a count from a rate, and explain what each tells a manager. Calculate conversion rate, average order value, revenue, returning-customer share and rating response rate from raw counts, naming the numerator and denominator of each. Compare a KPI with its target and direction, stating the gap in units, in percentage points or as a percentage of the target as appropriate. Classify measures as leading or lagging indicators and explain how a chain of them connects activity to results. Evaluate a set of KPIs for balance and for the risk of gaming that Goodhart’s law describes.

t: Summarising data: changes, averages and spread
s: B01 · Most business numbers are summaries: a share, a change, an average, a growth rate. Learn to calculate each one correctly, to say percentage points when you mean them, to choose between the mean and the median, to describe spread, to weight an average properly and to round without misleading.
x: Proportion Percentage change Percentage point Base effect Compound growth rate Mean Median Mode Range Quartile Interquartile range Standard deviation Weighted average Calculate proportions, percentages, absolute changes and percentage changes, and name the base of each. Distinguish a percentage-point change from a percentage change and calculate both. Calculate month-on-month growth rates and the compound average growth rate over several periods. Calculate the mean, median and mode, and describe spread with the range, the interquartile range and the standard deviation, choosing the summary that suits the data and the question. Calculate a weighted average, and explain why a shop’s overall conversion rate is a weighted average of its channels’ rates. State results to a precision the data support, rounding only at the end.

t: Interpreting results: charts, comparisons and causes
s: B01 · Numbers don’t interpret themselves. Learn to read a chart critically, to compare like with like, to tell correlation from causation, to spot Simpson’s paradox and regression to the mean, to diagnose why a KPI moved, and to write a finding that says how sure you are.
x: Seasonality Correlated Causation Confounding variable Comparison group Difference-in-differences Simpson’s paradox Regression to the mean Read a chart critically, checking its axes, where its vertical axis starts, its scale and its encoding, and calculate how much a truncated axis exaggerates a change. Compare like with like, adjusting for period length, base effects and seasonality. Distinguish correlation from causation, and identify confounding variables and the evidence that would support a causal claim. Explain Simpson’s paradox and regression to the mean, and recognise them in business data. Diagnose a change in a KPI by decomposing it into drivers and segments and comparing it with an unaffected group. Write a finding that states the change, the comparison, the evidence and the remaining uncertainty.

t: Datasets: rows, columns, records and variables
s: B02 · Before you clean or analyse a table, describe it exactly: what one row is, what kind of value each column holds, which column identifies each row, and what every column is supposed to contain. Get this wrong and correct arithmetic gives the wrong answer.
x: Dataset Observation Variable Unit of observation Tidy data Nominal variable Ordinal variable Interval variable Ratio variable Discrete variable Continuous variable Primary key Composite key Data dictionary Wide format Long format Identify the observations, variables and unit of observation of a dataset, and explain why the unit changes the answer to a question. Recognise tidy and untidy layouts, and describe what makes a layout untidy. Classify a variable as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio, and as discrete or continuous, and state which comparisons and summaries it supports. Choose a primary key or composite key for a table and test whether it identifies every row. Write a data dictionary entry that defines a column’s meaning, level, type, unit and rules. Distinguish wide and long layouts of the same data.

t: Profiling a dataset and writing validation rules
s: B02 · Find out what a dataset really contains before you change it: profile every column, name each problem by the quality dimension it affects, and turn what you find into precise validation rules and a cleaning plan.
x: Data profiling Data quality dimension Completeness Validity Accuracy Consistency Uniqueness Timeliness Validation rule Range check Format check Referential integrity Cross-field check Profile a dataset: its shape, types, blanks, distinct values, ranges, summary statistics and frequency tables, with cross-checks between columns. Classify a data problem by the quality dimension it affects: completeness, validity, accuracy, consistency, uniqueness or timeliness. Write validation rules of each kind (type, range, set membership, format, uniqueness, completeness, cross-field and referential integrity) and give each a severity. Calculate completeness, a rule’s failure rate and the share of rows that fail at least one rule. Explain why a value can pass every validation rule and still be wrong. Plan cleaning from a profile by turning its findings into a prioritised issue list before changing any data.

s: B02 · A record counted twice inflates revenue, customer numbers and averages without any warning. Learn to tell exact copies, conflicting versions and near duplicates apart, decide what counts as “the same” for the business, and remove duplicates without deleting genuine repeat orders.
x: Duplicate record Exact duplicate Near duplicate Business key Deduplication Survivorship rule Fuzzy matching Edit distance Distinguish exact duplicates, repeated keys with conflicting values and near duplicates, and explain how each kind arises. Identify the business key that defines “the same record” for a dataset, and the evidence that separates a duplicate from a genuine repeat. Choose a survivorship rule (first, latest update, most complete or merge) for a group of duplicates and justify it. Calculate how duplicates distort totals, counts and averages. Compute the edit distance between two short strings and explain how fuzzy matching uses it. Find duplicates with a spreadsheet, with SQL and with pandas.

t: Incorrect data types and inconsistent dates
s: B02 · A price stored as text won’t add up, and a date stored as text won’t sort. Learn to give every column the right data type, convert numbers written in different local formats, keep identifiers as text, and turn a column of mixed dates into unambiguous ISO 8601 dates without guessing.
x: Data type Type conversion Locale Leading zero Ambiguous date ISO 8601 Serial date UTC Identify the data type each column should have, and explain how a wrong type breaks sorting, sums and joins. Convert numbers stored as text, including currency symbols, thousands separators, decimal commas and negatives in parentheses. Recognise identifiers that look numeric but must stay text, such as codes with leading zeros. Convert dates in mixed formats to ISO 8601, resolving ambiguous dates with evidence rather than guesswork. Calculate the date behind a spreadsheet serial number, and the serial number of a date, in the 1900 date system. Explain how to store and report times so that time zones and daylight saving don’t corrupt them.

s: B02 · “North”, “north ”, “N.” and “Nrth” are one region to a person and four to a computer. Learn to normalise whitespace, case and Unicode, consolidate variants with a reviewed mapping table, split and extract fields with simple patterns, and see how consolidation changes counts and averages.
x: Whitespace Non-breaking space Code point Case normalisation Unicode normalisation Mapping table Controlled vocabulary Category consolidation Regular expression Identify the whitespace, case, punctuation and Unicode differences that make equal-looking text values unequal. Normalise text values by trimming, case normalisation and Unicode normalisation, in a sensible order. Build and maintain a mapping table that consolidates variants into a controlled vocabulary. Use simple regular expressions to check, extract and split text, and explain their limits. Calculate how category consolidation changes group counts and averages.

s: B02 · A blank cell is a question: why is the value missing? Learn to find every form missing data takes, judge whether the gaps are random, and choose between deleting and imputing without quietly biasing the answer.
x: Missing value MCAR MAR MNAR Listwise deletion Pairwise deletion Imputation Mean imputation Missing-value indicator Multiple imputation Recognise the forms missing data takes in an export, including placeholders such as 0, −999 and “unknown”, and blanks that really mean zero. Distinguish data missing completely at random, at random and not at random, and explain why the data alone cannot settle which applies. Calculate how deletion, mean imputation and group-wise imputation change a mean, a standard deviation and a correlation. Choose between deletion, single imputation, a missing-value indicator and multiple imputation for a stated purpose, and justify the choice. Apply imputation without leakage by computing fill values from training data only.

s: B02 · Some unusual values are mistakes, some are impossible and some are the most important rows in the file. Learn to flag them with quartile fences and robust z-scores, to see why the ordinary z-score can miss them, and to choose and document a treatment that fits the question.
x: Outlier Interquartile range Tukey fences Z-score Modified z-score Median absolute deviation Winsorising Masking Robust statistic Distinguish impossible values, errors and genuine extreme values, and explain why impossible values are a validation problem before they are an outlier problem. Calculate quartiles, the interquartile range, Tukey fences, z-scores and modified z-scores for a small dataset. Explain masking and why rules built on the median and the median absolute deviation resist it. Choose a treatment for a flagged value (correct, remove, cap, keep with robust statistics, or flag) and calculate its effect on the mean and the median. Document an outlier decision so that someone else could reproduce it.

s: B02 · Order values, hotel bills and study hours pile up at the low end and stretch out in a long tail. Learn to measure that skew, to see when it distorts summaries, outlier rules and models, and to transform a variable, read the results back in real units, and know when to leave it alone.
x: Skewness Right-skewed Left-skewed Log transformation Log1p transformation Square-root transformation Box–Cox transformation Geometric mean Calculate the sample skewness of a small dataset with the adjusted Fisher–Pearson coefficient and interpret its sign. Explain how skewness distorts means, outlier rules and models. Transform a skewed variable with a log, log(1 + x), square root or Box–Cox transformation, choosing one that suits its values. Interpret results after a log transformation, including log differences as approximate percentage changes and back-transformed means as geometric means. Decide when a variable should not be transformed.

s: B02 · Put numeric variables on comparable scales with min–max normalisation, standardisation and robust scaling, so that no variable dominates an analysis just because of its units. Learn which methods need scaling, what an outlier does to each scaler, and how to fit the scaling on training data only so that no test information leaks into the model.
x: Feature scaling Min–max normalisation Standardisation Robust scaling Data leakage Training set Test set Explain why distance-based, penalised and gradient-based methods need features on comparable scales, and when scaling makes no difference. Calculate min–max normalised, standardised and robust-scaled values, and convert scaled values back to the original units. Compare how an extreme value affects each scaler and choose a suitable method for a given variable. Distinguish the different meanings of “normalisation” and state precisely which transformation was used. Apply scaling without data leakage: fit the parameters on the training set and apply them unchanged to the test set and to new data. Interpret distances and regression coefficients computed from scaled variables.

s: B02 · Turn categories such as region, room type or roast into numbers a model can use, without inventing an order or a distance the categories don’t have. Learn one-hot and dummy coding, ordinal, frequency and target encoding, and how to handle the dummy-variable trap, rare and unseen categories, and variables with thousands of values.
x: Categorical encoding One-hot encoding Dummy variable Dummy-variable trap Reference category Ordinal encoding Label encoding Frequency encoding Target encoding High cardinality Explain why most models need categorical variables converted to numbers, and how arbitrary codes mislead linear and distance-based models. Encode a nominal variable with one-hot encoding or dummy coding, and calculate how many columns an encoding creates. Explain the dummy-variable trap and decide when dropping a reference category is necessary and when keeping every column is better. Apply ordinal, frequency and target encoding, and state the assumption each makes. Calculate smoothed and out-of-fold target encodings that avoid data leakage. Handle rare categories, categories unseen at prediction time and high-cardinality variables.

s: B02 · Clean data rarely arrives in the shape a question needs. Learn to derive new variables, sort values into bins, aggregate, reshape between wide and long, and join tables, and to check every step so that it adds information rather than errors.
x: Derived variable Binning Granularity Aggregation Weighted average Reshaping Pivot Melt Join Inner join Left join Full outer join Row explosion Construct derived variables (totals, ratios, flags, date parts and durations) and use them to check stored values. Compare equal-width, equal-frequency and business-defined bins, and explain what binning throws away. Calculate group summaries at a stated granularity, and distinguish the overall average from an average of group averages. Reshape a table between wide and long format, and explain which questions need each layout. Determine the row count of inner, left and full joins, including the row explosion caused by repeated keys. Design a repeatable sequence of transformations that leaves the raw data untouched.

t: Data quality reporting and a reproducible workflow
s: B02 · Cleaning is finished only when someone else can see what you did, why, and what it means for the results, and can repeat it. Learn to write a data quality report, keep a cleaning log, and run a reproducible workflow from the raw export to analysis-ready data.
x: Data quality report Raw data Cleaning log Reproducibility Data lineage Percentage point Data minimisation Pseudonymised Explain who reads a data quality report and what each reader needs from it. Write the sections of a data quality report, including each issue, the decision taken and its rationale, and the limitations that remain. Calculate before-and-after profile figures and describe how exclusions change who the data represent. Construct a reproducible cleaning workflow that keeps the raw data untouched and records its lineage. Evaluate reporting choices for honesty, bias and the protection of personal data.

s: B03 · A spreadsheet is only as trustworthy as its formulas. Learn how Excel reads a formula, how references move when a formula is filled or copied, why a number can look rounded without being rounded, what each error value means, and how to lay out a worksheet that someone else can check.
x: Cell reference Cell range Formula Relative reference Absolute reference Mixed reference Error value Circular reference Defined name Identify cells, ranges and references in a worksheet, and distinguish a typed value from a formula. Calculate what a formula returns using Excel’s order of operations, including negation and the percent sign. Build formulas with relative, absolute and mixed references that stay right when filled down and across. Explain the difference between a cell’s displayed value and its stored value, and decide when to round with ROUND. Diagnose the common error values and trace a formula’s precedents and dependents. Design a worksheet whose inputs are labelled and kept apart from its calculations, so that it can be checked.

s: B03 · Excel’s built-in functions do the heavy lifting: counting exactly what you mean, rounding by a business rule, making decisions with IF, taking text apart and joining it, and calculating with dates. Learn how each one works, where each one trips people up, and how to handle errors without hiding them.
x: Function Argument Logical value Nested function Text string Concatenation Write functions with the right syntax, arguments and nesting, and choose between SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK by exactly what each counts. Choose between ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, INT and MROUND to round by a business rule, and explain the choice. Build decisions with IF, nested IF, IFS, AND, OR and NOT, putting the conditions in the right order. Use IFERROR and IFNA to handle the errors you expect without hiding the ones you don’t. Use LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN, FIND, SEARCH, TRIM, SUBSTITUTE, TEXT and the & operator to split, clean and join text. Calculate with dates using DATE, YEAR, MONTH, DAY, EOMONTH, EDATE, WEEKDAY and NETWORKDAYS.

s: B03 · Most business questions about a table of transactions are “how much, how many, or how good, for the rows that meet a condition”. Learn SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS and SUMPRODUCT, the criteria that make them precise (operators, cell references, wildcards, blanks and date windows), and how to build a summary table with one formula.
x: Conditional aggregate Criterion Criteria range Wildcard character Summary table Write SUMIF, SUMIFS, COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIF, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS and MINIFS formulas that answer exactly the question asked. Construct criteria with comparison operators, cell references, wildcards and blanks, including a date window made of two criteria. Combine conditions with AND logic (several criteria) and OR logic (adding conditional sums, or SUMPRODUCT), without counting any row twice. Calculate weighted totals and averages, and conditional totals, with SUMPRODUCT. Build a two-way summary table with mixed references so that one formula fills it, and reconcile it with the data’s grand total.

t: Lookups: VLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, XLOOKUP
s: B03 · Bring a value from one table into another by matching a key: a product’s cost from a price list, a delivery charge from a table of bands. Learn VLOOKUP, INDEX and MATCH, and XLOOKUP, when to match exactly and when approximately, and how to find out why a lookup returns #N/A or, worse, a wrong answer.
x: Lookup value Lookup table Exact match Approximate match Two-way lookup Spill Use VLOOKUP with an exact match to bring a value from a lookup table into a list, and explain why leaving out its fourth argument is a trap. Build INDEX and MATCH lookups, including lookups to the left of the key and two-way lookups by a row and a column label. Use XLOOKUP and XMATCH with a not-found value, match modes and search modes, and state which versions of Excel have them. Apply approximate-match lookups to band tables such as delivery charges, and test the boundaries of every band. Diagnose lookups that return #N/A or a wrong value because of spaces, numbers stored as text, misspellings, missing keys or duplicate keys.

s: B03 · Turn a range into an Excel table, so that formulas refer to columns by name and grow with the data; sort, filter and validate it; and clean an imported export with TRIM, VALUE, DATE and the dynamic array functions, keeping the raw data untouched and every step on record.
x: Excel table Structured reference Calculated column Total row Data validation Dynamic array function Power Query Build an Excel table, and write structured references, calculated columns and a total row. Use sorting, filtering, data validation and Remove Duplicates, and explain what each one does to the data. Clean imported text, numbers and dates with TRIM, CLEAN, PROPER, SUBSTITUTE, VALUE, DATEVALUE and DATE, keeping the raw data untouched and logging each step. Choose between formulas, Text to Columns, Flash Fill, Find and Replace and Power Query for a cleaning job. Use UNIQUE, SORT, SORTBY and FILTER, and explain spill ranges and the #SPILL! error.

s: B03 · Summarise hundreds of rows by dragging fields: order value by month and channel, events by type, each item’s share of a total. Learn how a PivotTable groups and aggregates its source, how to show percentages and months, how to keep it up to date, and when SUMIFS formulas are the better choice.
x: PivotTable Pivot cache Slicer Distinct count Prepare source data for a PivotTable, and explain why an Excel table is the best source. Build PivotTables with fields in the Rows, Columns, Values and Filters areas, choosing Sum, Count, Average, Max or Min. Use Show Values As to give percentages of the grand total, the column total and the row total, and interpret each correctly. Use date grouping, sorting and filtering on a PivotTable, and refresh it after its source data change. Compare a PivotTable with SUMIFS and COUNTIFS formulas, reconcile one against the other, and choose the right tool for a report.

s: B03 · A chart or a highlighted cell should answer one question at a glance. Choose the chart from the question, build it honestly in Excel (a title that states the finding, bars from zero, colour that never carries the meaning alone), and use conditional formatting, including formula rules with mixed references, to make the cells that matter stand out.
x: Data series Category axis Value axis Scatter chart Box and whisker chart Combo chart Secondary axis Sparkline Truncated axis Contrast ratio Conditional formatting Data bar Colour scale Icon set Choose a chart type from the question it must answer: a comparison, a change over time, a composition, a distribution or a relationship. Build an Excel chart whose title states the finding, with labelled axes, units and direct labels, and calculate the figures it needs, such as shares of a total. Evaluate a chart’s scales and colours: bars from zero, when a line chart may zoom, the risks of truncated and secondary axes, and colour that is never the only cue. Apply Excel’s conditional formatting rules (highlight cells, top/bottom, above average, duplicates, data bars, colour scales and icon sets) and explain what each one compares. Write formula-based conditional formatting rules with mixed references that highlight whole rows, and manage rule order and Stop If True.

t: Descriptive statistics and regression in Excel
s: B03 · Describe a column of numbers with Excel’s statistics functions and the Analysis ToolPak, see what one large order does to the mean and the standard deviation, build a frequency table, and fit a straight line through catering invoices. Then read every line of the ToolPak’s regression output, and say what it does and doesn’t show.
x: Variance Standard error of the mean Kurtosis Percentile Bin Analysis ToolPak Correlation coefficient Regression line Least-squares line Residual R squared Standard error of the regression Extrapolation P-value 95% confidence interval Calculate the mean, median, mode, standard deviation, variance, quartiles and percentiles of a column with Excel functions, choosing STDEV.S or STDEV.P and the .INC or .EXC quartile deliberately. Read the Analysis ToolPak’s Descriptive Statistics report and explain what its Standard Error, Kurtosis, Skewness and Confidence Level lines measure. Build a frequency table with FREQUENCY or COUNTIFS, and explain which bin Excel puts a value on a bin edge in. Explain how one extreme value moves the mean, the standard deviation and a regression line but not the median. Calculate CORREL, SLOPE, INTERCEPT, RSQ and FORECAST.LINEAR, and add a trendline with its equation and R² to a scatter chart. Interpret the ToolPak’s Regression output for a simple regression (R Square, Standard Error, Significance F, coefficients, p-values and 95% limits) without claiming more than it shows.

t: What-if analysis: data tables, Goal Seek, scenarios and Solver
s: B03 · A well-built model answers questions. Use one to see how a catering job’s contribution responds to guests, hours and costs (data tables and scenarios), to find the price that reaches a target margin (Goal Seek), and to choose the month’s best mix of events and workshops within limited time (Solver).
x: What-if analysis Contribution margin Sensitivity analysis Data table Scenario Manager Goal Seek Solver Decision variable Objective Constraint Linear programme Feasible region Integer constraint Binding constraint Slack Shadow price Build a what-if model with inputs, calculations and outputs separated, one assumption per cell and no typed-in numbers in its formulas. Use one- and two-variable data tables, sensitivity analysis and Scenario Manager to show how an output responds to its inputs. Use Goal Seek to find the input that makes a formula reach a target, and check its answer by algebra. Construct a linear programme for a decision (decision variables, objective, constraints) and solve it with Solver’s Simplex LP method, with and without integer constraints. Interpret Solver’s results: binding constraints, slack, shadow prices, and infeasible or unbounded models. Evaluate a model’s answers with independent checks before acting on them.

s: B03 · A dashboard is one page that tells its readers where things stand. Learn to start from the audience’s questions, give every number a comparison, lay the page out so the most important measure comes first, build it on tables, formulas and PivotTables so it refreshes, and add the documentation and checks that make it trustworthy.
x: Client concentration Visual hierarchy Drop-down list Timeline Reconciliation check Year to date Identify a dashboard’s audience and questions, and choose the measures that answer them, each with a definition, a comparison and an owner. Design a one-page layout that puts the most important measure first, with consistent scales, formats and labels and a fitting display for each question. Build dashboard figures with SUMIFS, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS and XLOOKUP driven by a drop-down cell, and with PivotTables, slicers and timelines on one table of data. Document a dashboard’s sources, definitions and refresh date, and add reconciliation checks that prove it agrees with its data. Evaluate a dashboard for common failures and accessibility problems, and plan how it is shared and kept under version control.

s: B04 · Before you infer anything from data, describe it exactly: its centre, its spread, where a value sits within it and its shape. Learn the notation that separates a population from a sample, why the sample variance divides by n − 1, what z-scores, percentile ranks and the coefficient of variation say, and when the empirical rule or only Chebyshev’s inequality applies.
x: Parameter Statistic Sum of squares Degrees of freedom Trimmed mean Coefficient of variation Percentile rank Empirical rule Chebyshev’s inequality Five-number summary Distinguish a population parameter (μ, σ, N) from a sample statistic (x̄, s, n), and explain why the sample variance divides by n − 1. Calculate the mean, median, trimmed mean, variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation by hand and in Excel, and predict how adding a constant or changing units moves each of them. Locate a value within its group with a z-score and a percentile rank, using STANDARDIZE, PERCENTRANK.INC and COUNTIF. Decide whether the empirical rule or Chebyshev’s inequality applies to a distribution, and apply it. Describe a distribution’s shape with the five-number summary, a box plot, SKEW and KURT, and a categorical variable with counts, proportions and the mode. Compare several groups side by side with summaries that suit their shape.

s: B04 · Probability is the language every test and interval in this course is written in. Learn to read joint, marginal and conditional probabilities from a contingency table, to use the addition and multiplication rules, to check whether two events are independent, to draw a tree diagram, and to turn a screen’s accuracy into the probability that a flagged case is real with Bayes’ rule.
x: Sample space Event Probability Relative frequency Law of large numbers Contingency table Joint probability Marginal probability Conditional probability Complement Mutually exclusive Independent Tree diagram Bayes’ rule Base rate False positive Define an experiment, its sample space and its events, and distinguish classical, relative-frequency and subjective probability. Calculate joint, marginal and conditional probabilities from a contingency table, and the probability of a complement, a union and an intersection. Decide whether two events are independent by comparing P(A | B) with P(A), and say what independence would predict for a table. Use a tree diagram and the multiplication rule for events in sequence, with and without replacement. Apply Bayes’ rule to a screening problem, explaining the role of the base rate and of false positives. Calculate the number of possible samples and arrangements with COMBIN and PERMUT.
