s: B04 · Many business questions are about counts: subscriptions among the next orders, orders on a day, boxes sold at a market. Learn to describe a count with a probability distribution, its expected value and its standard deviation, to recognise the binomial and Poisson distributions and check their conditions, and to calculate their probabilities by hand and with BINOM.DIST and POISSON.DIST.
x: Random variable Probability distribution Binomial distribution Poisson distribution Exponential distribution Describe a discrete random variable with a probability distribution, and calculate its expected value, variance and standard deviation. Identify when a count follows a binomial distribution, and calculate binomial probabilities, the mean np and the standard deviation √(np(1 − p)) by hand and with BINOM.DIST and BINOM.DIST.RANGE. Identify when a count follows a Poisson distribution, calculate its probabilities with POISSON.DIST, and compare observed counts with a Poisson model. Explain when the Poisson approximates the binomial, and how the exponential distribution describes the time between Poisson events. Use expected values and standard deviations to compare decisions under uncertainty.

s: B04 · Model a measurement with the normal curve: turn values into z-scores, find the share of bags under a label weight and the machine setting that keeps it below 1%, with NORM.DIST and NORM.INV and by hand. Then check whether the model fits, and see where it fails.
x: Probability density function Normal distribution Standard normal distribution Normal probability plot Continuity correction Explain how a probability density curve gives probabilities as areas, and why the probability of one exact value of a continuous variable is 0. Calculate z-scores and normal probabilities below, above, between and outside given values, by hand from z and with NORM.DIST, NORM.S.DIST and STANDARDIZE. Find the value that cuts off a given probability with NORM.INV and NORM.S.INV, and use it to set a target such as a machine setting or a stock level. Assess whether a normal model is reasonable for a dataset with a histogram, the mean and median, the empirical-rule counts, SKEW and KURT, and a normal probability plot. Recognise data, such as right-skewed order values, for which a normal model gives wrong answers. Use the normal approximation to the binomial with a continuity correction, and state when it is adequate.

s: B04 · A sample’s mean or proportion changes from one sample to the next. See how much, through the standard error σ ÷ √n and the central limit theorem, on Lantern’s strongly skewed spring orders; use the normal model for a sample mean, and know when it misleads. Then compare the ways of drawing a sample and the biases that no sample size cures.
x: Sampling distribution Standard error Central limit theorem Finite population correction Systematic sample Stratified sample Cluster sample Distinguish a parameter from a statistic, and explain what a sampling distribution is. Calculate the standard error of a sample mean and of a sample proportion, with the finite population correction when the sample is a large share of the population. Explain the central limit theorem, and judge how large a sample must be for a sample mean to be close to normal when the population is skewed. Calculate probabilities for a sample mean or proportion with the normal model, and recognise when that model is unreliable. Compare simple random, systematic, stratified and cluster samples, and identify the biases that a larger sample does not remove.

s: B04 · Turn a sample’s mean or proportion into a range for the population’s, with a margin of error that says how far it could be off. Build z and t intervals for a mean and an interval for a proportion, by hand and with CONFIDENCE.NORM and CONFIDENCE.T; say exactly what “95% confident” means; and work out the sample a margin needs.
x: Point estimate Confidence interval Confidence level Margin of error t distribution Wilson interval Explain a confidence interval as an estimate plus or minus a margin of error, and interpret a 95% confidence level correctly. Calculate a z interval for a mean when σ is known and a t interval when it isn’t, by hand and with CONFIDENCE.NORM, CONFIDENCE.T and T.INV.2T. Explain why the t distribution is used when σ is estimated, and how its degrees of freedom change it. Calculate an interval for a proportion, check its conditions, and recognise when the Wilson interval is the better choice. Describe how the confidence level, the spread and the sample size change the margin of error, and calculate the sample size a margin needs for a mean or a proportion. Identify what an interval doesn’t cover: bias from non-response or from a non-random sample, and the spread of individual values.

s: B04 · Compare two means the way the data were collected: with a paired t test when the same units are measured twice, and with Welch’s t test when the groups are separate. Run both by hand, with T.TEST and with the Analysis ToolPak, put an interval and an effect size on the difference, and check the conditions before trusting any of it.
x: Independent samples Paired samples Two-sample t test Welch’s t test Pooled t test Paired t test F test for equal variances Effect size Cohen’s d Mann–Whitney U test Wilcoxon signed-rank test Choose between a paired and an independent-samples test from how the data were collected, and explain why pairing can reveal a difference that a two-sample test misses. Calculate Welch’s and the pooled two-sample t statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value by hand and with T.TEST types 1 to 3, and explain why Welch’s test is the safer default. Read the Analysis ToolPak’s three t-test outputs, including the one- and two-tail rows and the rounded degrees of freedom of the unequal-variances tool. Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a difference in means and for a mean difference, and report an effect size with Cohen’s d. Assess independence, normality or sample size, and outliers before a comparison, and recognise when a rank test such as Mann–Whitney or Wilcoxon’s is worth considering.

s: B04 · Compare two proportions with a z test and a confidence interval, then use the chi-square distribution to test whether counts fit a model and whether two categorical variables are related. Calculate each test by hand and in Excel with CHISQ.TEST, CHISQ.DIST.RT and CHISQ.INV.RT, check its conditions, and say what a result does and doesn’t show.
x: Two-proportion z test Pooled proportion Expected count Chi-square statistic Chi-square distribution Goodness-of-fit test Test of independence Cramér’s V Calculate a two-proportion z test with the pooled standard error and a confidence interval for the difference in two proportions, and check their conditions. Describe the chi-square distribution and explain why chi-square tests use the right tail and how their degrees of freedom are counted. Test whether counts fit a stated model with a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, including a model whose parameter is estimated from the data, merging categories whose expected counts are too small. Test for independence in a contingency table: expected counts, the chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom, the p-value and the expected-count condition. Calculate chi-square tests in Excel with CHISQ.TEST, CHISQ.DIST.RT and CHISQ.INV.RT, and recognise when CHISQ.TEST uses the wrong degrees of freedom. Interpret a result with percentages, an interval or Cramér’s V, without treating a non-significant result as no difference or an association as a cause.

s: B04 · Compare the means of several groups at once without inflating the chance of a false alarm. Split variation into between- and within-group parts, build the F statistic by hand and with Excel’s Anova: Single Factor, check the conditions, measure the effect with η², and find which groups differ with adjusted comparisons.
x: Analysis of variance Family-wise error rate Between-group variation Within-group variation Mean square F statistic F distribution Eta squared Bonferroni correction Explain why comparing several means with a t test for every pair inflates the family-wise error rate, and calculate that rate. Calculate the between-group and within-group sums of squares, degrees of freedom, mean squares and F for a one-way ANOVA, by hand and with DEVSQ. Use Excel’s Anova: Single Factor and read its SUMMARY and ANOVA tables, finding p-values and critical values with F.DIST.RT and F.INV.RT. Assess the conditions of one-way ANOVA (independence, normality, equal variances) and choose a response when they fail, such as Welch’s ANOVA. Interpret a significant or non-significant F with η², and identify which groups differ with Bonferroni-adjusted comparisons or Tukey’s HSD.

s: M01 · Marketing is not advertising with a bigger budget. Learn how marketers define it, why a voluntary exchange creates value for both sides, how needs, wants and demand differ, why defining a business by its product is dangerous, and what marketing looks like in consumer, business, service and non-profit settings.
x: Marketing Exchange (marketing) Willingness to pay Need Want Demand Market offering Market Customer Consumer Marketing myopia Marketing process Customer equity Business-to-consumer Business-to-business Explain what marketing is, using the American Marketing Association’s definition and a scholarly alternative, and why it is more than advertising and selling. Distinguish needs, wants and demand, and identify the market offering that answers them. Calculate the value an exchange creates and how the price divides it between buyer and seller. Recognise marketing myopia and restate a business in terms of the customer need it serves. Describe the five steps of the marketing process and what marketers do at each. Compare marketing in consumer, business, service and non-profit settings.

t: Customer value, satisfaction and lifetime value
s: M01 · Customers choose the offer they judge best value, stay if it meets the expectations they formed, and are worth what they bring in over the years they stay. Learn customer-perceived value, satisfaction and loyalty, how to calculate a simple customer lifetime value with its assumptions stated, how to compare it with the cost of winning a customer, and how to write a value proposition.
x: Customer value Customer satisfaction Expectation disconfirmation Customer loyalty Retention rate Churn rate Customer lifetime value Customer acquisition cost Contribution margin Value proposition Explain customer-perceived value as benefits weighed against money and non-money costs, and why the customer’s judgement is the one that counts. Explain satisfaction as perceived performance measured against expectations, and how it relates to loyalty and retention. Calculate a customer’s lifetime value from margin, retention and a discount rate, stating the assumptions about timing and horizon. Compare lifetime value with the cost of acquiring a customer to judge whether acquisition or retention spending pays. Evaluate a value proposition: whom it is for, what it promises, and why that beats the alternatives.

t: Market orientation: putting customers at the centre
s: M01 · Businesses differ in what they start from: what they can make, how good the product is, how hard they sell, or what customers need. Learn the five classic orientations and their limits, what a market orientation requires in practice (intelligence about customers and competitors, shared across the business and acted on), how to read what customers tell you, and why ethics and society belong in the picture.
x: Production concept Product concept Selling concept Marketing concept Societal marketing concept Market orientation Market intelligence Customer orientation Competitor orientation Inter-functional coordination Customer-centric Greenwashing Distinguish the production, product, selling, marketing and societal marketing concepts by what each starts from and what it risks. Explain market orientation as behaviour, using Kohli and Jaworski’s three activities and Narver and Slater’s three components. Compare customer-centric and product-centric organisations and the measures each relies on. Calculate the share of respondents giving each reason in customer research, and interpret what such figures can and cannot show. Evaluate a marketing decision for its effects on society, using the AMA’s ethical norms and the rules on environmental claims.

s: M01 · Every purchase, from a bag of beans to a barista course, comes out of a decision, made in seconds or over weeks. Learn the five stages of the buying process, how involvement changes it, how buyers weigh alternatives (with a scoring model you can calculate), what happens after the sale, and where the tidy model breaks down, online and off.
x: Buying decision process Need recognition Information search Consideration set Weighted-attribute model Non-compensatory rule Post-purchase dissonance Involvement Complex buying behaviour Dissonance-reducing buying behaviour Habitual buying behaviour Variety-seeking buying behaviour Touchpoint Customer journey Describe the five stages of the consumer buying process and what a marketer can do at each one. Distinguish high- from low-involvement purchases and classify buying behaviour as complex, dissonance-reducing, habitual or variety-seeking. Calculate weighted-attribute scores for competing offers and the improvement an offer needs to draw level with the leader. Explain post-purchase dissonance and how sellers can reduce it. Evaluate the limits of linear decision models, including the way online journeys loop, skip stages and add options.

s: M01 · Why do two people with the same need buy different things? Learn the cultural, social, personal and psychological influences on a purchase; what motivation, perception, learning and attitudes mean; why word of mouth carries so much weight; and how anchoring, defaults and loss aversion shape choices, with the evidence and the ethics of using them.
x: Culture Subculture Social class Reference group Opinion leader Word of mouth Lifestyle Motive Maslow’s hierarchy of needs Perception Selective attention Attitude Anchoring Default effect Loss aversion Referral multiplier Nudge Dark pattern Classify influences on a purchase as cultural, social, personal or psychological. Explain motivation, perception, learning and attitudes, and evaluate Maslow’s hierarchy of needs against the evidence. Explain how reference groups, opinion leaders and word of mouth affect choices, and calculate a simple referral multiplier. Define anchoring, the default effect and loss aversion accurately and recognise them in prices and online-shop design. Evaluate whether a use of behavioural insight serves customers or exploits them.

s: M01 · Organisations buy differently from households: their demand is derived from their own customers’, they are fewer and larger, purchasing is a profession, and several people share each decision. Learn the three buying situations, the six roles in a buying centre, the stages of the business buying process and the procurement rules that decide how a seller must sell.
x: Business market Derived demand Acceleration effect Straight rebuy Modified rebuy New task Buying centre Initiator (buying centre) User (buying centre) Influencer (buying centre) Buyer (buying centre) Decider (buying centre) Gatekeeper (buying centre) Business buying process Request for proposal Total cost of ownership Approval limit Approved supplier list Compare business and consumer markets, and calculate how a change in end demand is amplified in orders for equipment. Classify purchases as straight rebuys, modified rebuys or new tasks, and explain what each means for the current supplier and a challenger. Identify the roles in a buying centre (initiators, users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers) from what people do in a purchase. Describe the stages of the business buying process and the procurement rules that govern it. Recommend how a seller should approach an organisational buyer.

s: M01 · Before deciding where to go, a business needs an honest picture of where it stands. Learn to scan the marketing environment with PESTEL, profile competitors and compare them with numbers, and build a SWOT analysis that rests on evidence and leads to decisions, knowing what each tool can and can’t tell you.
x: Situation analysis Marketing environment Microenvironment Macroenvironment PESTEL Competitor analysis Substitute Market share Weighted competitive-strength scorecard SWOT analysis TOWS matrix Distinguish the microenvironment from the macroenvironment, and classify environmental factors with PESTEL. Analyse competitors, including indirect competitors and substitutes, and compare them with market share and a weighted competitive-strength scorecard. Construct a SWOT analysis that separates internal from external factors and supports each factor with evidence. Evaluate the evidence behind a situation analysis, including small samples and research drawn only from current customers. Explain the known weaknesses of SWOT and PESTEL, and use the TOWS matrix to turn a SWOT into strategic options.

s: M01 · A business goal says where the business wants to be; a marketing objective says which customers must do what, by when, to get it there. Learn to turn a goal into SMART objectives across the funnel, and to work out how many new customers a growth target really needs once you allow for the customers you lose.
x: Business goal Marketing objective Marketing strategy Marketing funnel Win rate Distinguish business goals, marketing objectives, strategies and tactics, and explain how each one serves the one above it. Write SMART marketing objectives and test objectives against the five criteria. Set objectives for each stage of the marketing funnel, from awareness to advocacy, with a measure for each. Calculate how many new customers a revenue target needs, given retention and revenue per customer. Calculate the leads or enquiries needed to win a number of customers, from the funnel’s conversion rates. Evaluate whether a set of objectives is consistent, achievable and protected against gaming.

s: M01 · Customers choose between alternatives, so a business needs a reason to be chosen that rivals can’t easily copy. Learn where competitive advantage comes from (lower cost, differentiation and focus), how to compare competing on price with competing on value, and how to judge whether an advantage will last.
x: Competitive advantage Value created Generic strategies Cost leadership Differentiation Focus Stuck in the middle Price premium Sustained competitive advantage VRIO Positioning Explain competitive advantage as creating more value than rivals, using willingness to pay, price and cost. Distinguish Porter’s generic strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, cost focus and differentiation focus) and classify businesses by the strategy they follow. Calculate a price premium and the highest price a difference in customer value can support against a rival. Compare competing on price with competing on value, including the risks of price wars and of being stuck in the middle. Evaluate whether a resource or capability can give a sustained advantage, using VRIO. Explain how positioning communicates a competitive advantage to target customers.

t: The marketing mix and customer value
s: M02 · Marketing turns an idea into an offer that people choose over the alternatives. Learn what customer value is, how product, price, place and promotion each create or capture it, and how to test whether a plan’s four decisions fit each other and the customers they are meant for.
x: Marketing Customer value Target market Positioning Value proposition Marketing mix 4Ps 4Cs 7Ps Explain what marketing is and what customer value means, in your own words and in the American Marketing Association’s. Classify marketing decisions as product, price, place or promotion decisions. Analyse whether the four decisions in a plan are consistent with each other and with the target market and positioning. Calculate how a price and a channel together determine what a business keeps per unit, and what a customer gives up to buy. Compare the 4Ps with the 4Cs and the 7Ps, and describe how the mix differs between business and consumer markets.

s: M02 · A product is a bundle of benefits, not just a thing. Learn to analyse an offer by its levels and attributes, classify it by how people buy it, describe a company’s product lines, and work out what quality and range decisions cost, using Lantern Cold Brew’s liquid, flavours and can.
x: Product Core benefit Actual product Augmented product Brand Packaging Convenience product Shopping product Specialty product Unsought product Product line Product mix Product mix width Product line length Product line depth Product mix consistency Line extension Distinguish the core benefit, the actual product and the augmented product of an offer. Classify consumer products as convenience, shopping, specialty or unsought products, and explain what each class implies for price, place and promotion. Describe a company’s product mix by its width, line length, depth and consistency, and explain line stretching, line filling and line extension. Calculate the cost consequences of quality and range decisions, including the cost-of-goods difference between tiers and the extra listing fees of a wider range. Evaluate a product decision against the positioning, the other three Ps and the costs it creates.

s: M02 · Products, like markets, tend to be born, grow, mature and fade, and each stage asks for a different mix. Learn the stages, the decisions that typically fit each one, how to read a product’s stage from data, and why the life cycle is a planning hypothesis rather than a law.
x: Product life cycle Introduction stage Growth stage Maturity stage Decline stage Style Fashion Fad Describe the four stages of the product life cycle and the typical sales, profit, customers and competition in each. Choose objectives and 4P decisions that fit a product’s stage, and explain when the typical prescription would not fit. Distinguish the life cycles of a product category, a product form and a brand, and of styles, fashions and fads. Calculate year-on-year growth and seasonally adjusted sales, and use them to judge which stage a product is in. Evaluate ways to extend a mature product’s life, and assess the criticisms of the life-cycle concept.

s: M02 · Price is the only part of the mix that brings money in. Learn to separate fixed from variable costs, work with contribution, markups and margins, find the break-even volume, and set a price between the floor your costs set and the ceiling your customers’ alternatives set.
x: Fixed cost Variable cost Contribution margin Break-even point Cost-plus pricing Markup Margin Target-return pricing Value-based pricing Competition-based pricing Price floor Price ceiling Classify costs as fixed or variable and calculate the contribution margin per unit and as a ratio of price. Convert between a markup on cost and a margin on price, and set the price that achieves a target margin. Calculate the break-even volume, the break-even revenue and the volume needed for a target profit. Apply cost-plus, target-return, value-based and competition-based pricing, and explain what each one leaves out. Identify a product’s price floor and price ceiling and use them, with competitors’ prices, to judge a proposed price.

s: M02 · How much do sales change when the price changes, and does the change pay? Measure price elasticity, predict what happens to revenue and to contribution, choose a launch price strategy, and use psychological, promotional, bundled and segmented prices within their evidence and their legal limits.
x: Demand curve Price elasticity of demand Elastic demand Inelastic demand Midpoint formula Price skimming Penetration pricing Psychological pricing Reference price Bundling Price discrimination Calculate price elasticity of demand with the point and midpoint formulas and classify demand as elastic, inelastic or unit-elastic. Determine the direction of a revenue change from the elasticity, and explain what makes demand more or less elastic. Calculate the volume change a price change needs to keep total contribution unchanged, and explain why a price cut that raises revenue can lower profit. Choose between skimming and penetration pricing for a new product and justify the choice with evidence. Evaluate charm prices, reference prices, discounts, bundling and price discrimination against the research evidence and their legal and ethical limits.

s: M02 · A product sells only where shoppers can find it. Learn what intermediaries do, how channels are structured, how much reach costs in margin and fees, and how to choose channels that fit the product, its price and its positioning.
x: Marketing channel Intermediary Wholesaler Distributor Retailer Agent or broker Channel level Direct channel Indirect channel Multichannel distribution Omnichannel Intensive distribution Selective distribution Exclusive distribution Trade margin Price build-up Slotting fee Channel conflict Logistics Explain the functions intermediaries perform and why removing an intermediary does not remove its work. Describe channel levels and distinguish direct, indirect, multichannel and omnichannel distribution. Choose a distribution intensity (intensive, selective or exclusive) that fits a product’s class and positioning. Calculate a price build-up from shelf price to net price and gross margin per unit, including trade margins, fulfilment costs and listing fees. Identify horizontal and vertical channel conflict and explain where channel power comes from. Evaluate channel options for a launch by comparing reach, margin per unit, fixed fees and fit with the positioning.

t: The promotion mix and integrated marketing communications
s: M02 · Promotion is how a business gets its offer noticed, understood and tried. Learn what each promotion tool does well and badly, when to push through the channel or pull through demand, how to make the messages work as one, and how to build a budget from objectives instead of guessing.
x: Promotion mix Advertising Sales promotion Trade promotion Personal selling Public relations Direct and digital marketing Push strategy Pull strategy AIDA Hierarchy-of-effects model Integrated marketing communications Affordable method Percentage-of-sales method Competitive-parity method Objective-and-task method Describe marketing communication as a process and explain where messages fail. Compare advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and direct and digital marketing by reach, cost per contact, persuasiveness and control. Distinguish push and pull strategies and classify promotion activities as one or the other. Evaluate response-hierarchy models such as AIDA and explain their limits. Calculate promotion budgets with the affordable, percentage-of-sales, competitive-parity and objective-and-task methods, and compare them. Plan an integrated launch campaign that is consistent with the product, price and channels.

t: Measuring promotion and bringing the mix together
s: M02 · Marketing numbers are easy to collect and easy to misread. Learn the media and digital metrics, why ROAS is not ROI, how to find out what promotion actually caused, and how to check that product, price, place and promotion work as one plan.
x: Impressions Reach Frequency Gross rating points CPM CTR CPC Conversion rate CPA ROAS Marketing ROI Break-even ROAS Incrementality Holdout group Attribution Test market Calculate reach, average frequency, gross rating points, CPM, CTR, conversion rate and CPA from campaign data. Distinguish ROAS from marketing ROI and show how a campaign with a high ROAS can lose money. Explain incrementality and design a holdout or A/B test that measures it. Identify the bias in last-click attribution and in other correlational evidence from marketing data. Choose a small set of dashboard metrics that match a plan’s objectives. Evaluate a marketing mix for consistency across product, price, place and promotion.

s: What finance is and how it differs from accounting and economics, the principles behind every financial decision, the vocabulary professionals use, and how financial markets and their participants work.
x: What finance is: time and risk Personal, corporate and investment finance Finance, accounting and economics Six decision principles: time value, risk and return, cash, incremental cash flows, diversification, no arbitrage Essential vocabulary: capital, liquidity, valuation, market capitalisation, enterprise value, EBITDA, working capital Interest and inflation Types of financial markets: equity, bond, foreign exchange, commodity, derivatives Market participants: investment banks, institutional investors, hedge funds, brokers How markets channel savings into investment

s: How a business records what happens to it: the accounting equation, debits and credits, journals and ledgers, adjustments, and the full accounting cycle.
Build all four financial statements and see how every transaction flows through them.

s: Interest, present and future value, annuities, loans and inflation, with every formula worked step by step.

s: Which projects to fund, what capital costs, how to finance the business and what to pay shareholders.

s: Risk and return, diversification, CAPM, bonds and equity valuation.

s: Risk management, derivatives and hedging, mergers, valuation and decisions under uncertainty.

s: Turn a messy export into data you can trust: profile it, fix records and formats, handle missing and unusual values, and prepare it for analysis without biasing the result.
